reference.source: ATS/ERS statements on eosinophilic lung disease / Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: Presents as an acute febrile hypoxaemic illness developing over days, often mimicking severe community-acquired pneumonia or acute respiratory distress syndrome
Frequently associated with recent initiation or resumption of tobacco smoking, or with new inhalational exposures
Peripheral blood eosinophilia is often absent at presentation, so a normal blood count does not exclude the diagnosis
The key diagnostic finding is marked eosinophilia on bronchoalveolar lavage, typically well above a quarter of the differential count
Imaging shows bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacity and consolidation, frequently with interlobular septal thickening and small pleural effusions
Infection and other causes of acute lung injury must be excluded before attributing the picture to idiopathic acute eosinophilic pneumonia
Response to corticosteroids is rapid and dramatic, with resolution and, unlike the chronic form, little tendency to relapse
Relapse is uncommon provided any provoking exposure such as smoking is avoided
reference.pathophysiology: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia is thought to represent an acute hypersensitivity reaction of the lung, often triggered by a new inhalational insult such as recently started cigarette smoking or dust exposure. There is rapid recruitment and activation of eosinophils within the alveoli and interstitium, with release of granule proteins and cytokines that produce diffuse alveolar damage and a capillary leak. This results in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure with bilateral infiltrates and effusions. Because the process is inflammatory rather than fibrotic and highly steroid responsive, it typically resolves completely without long-term sequelae.
additionalDifferentials: Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes
Parasitic (e.g. Loeffler-type) or fungal eosinophilic infiltration
additionalInvestigations: Bronchoalveolar lavage demonstrating marked eosinophilia as the central diagnostic test
High-resolution CT showing diffuse ground-glass opacity, consolidation, septal thickening, and pleural effusions
Full blood count with differential, recognising that peripheral eosinophilia may be delayed or absent
Detailed exposure history including recent smoking initiation and inhaled dusts or drugs
Microbiological workup to exclude infection before attributing the illness to eosinophilic pneumonia
Arterial blood gas or oximetry to quantify the degree of hypoxaemia
redFlags: Severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure that may require ventilatory support
Rapid clinical deterioration over hours to days
Failure to improve promptly with corticosteroids, prompting reconsideration of infection or another cause
New relevant inhalational exposure suggesting risk of recurrence if not avoided
reference.prognosis: With prompt corticosteroid treatment the prognosis is excellent, with rapid and usually complete recovery and, in contrast to chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, little tendency to relapse if the provoking exposure is removed.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because the peripheral blood eosinophil count is normal
Treating as refractory bacterial pneumonia or ARDS and delaying bronchoalveolar lavage
Overlooking a recent change in smoking behaviour or inhalational exposure as the trigger
Failing to exclude infection before starting corticosteroids
